title: Experimental narratives: A comparison of human crowdsourced storytelling and AI storytelling
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether prompted storytelling can be used as a controlled experimental method for comparing human and large language model (LLM) narrative generation, and what such a comparison reveals about cultural imaginaries and social bias. The author focuses on a specific fictional trope from the Pygmalion myth: a human creating an artificial human and then falling in love with it. The paper examines themes, gender and sexuality, race and ethnicity, and narrative quality across human and AI outputs.

The human data come from 250 Amazon Mechanical Turk crowdworkers who completed a story-writing task in June 2019. The AI data come from 80 stories generated in March 2023 by OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 using the same prompts; 50 additional Llama 3 70B outputs are mentioned as a comparison point, but the main analysis centers on the human-versus-GPT comparison. Participants were adult U.S.-based English speakers, and the setting was online. The study combines quantitative analysis, including counts and logistic regression on character gender and race, with qualitative narratological reading of story structure and motifs.

The paper concludes that both humans and LLMs readily reproduce the Pygmalion trope, showing how deeply it is embedded in cultural imagination. Human stories were more varied and often more imaginative, while GPT stories were more homogeneous, morally framed, and conventionally structured. At the same time, newer GPT models, especially GPT-4, showed more gender and sexual diversity than human stories and sometimes challenged traditional gender roles more than the human writers did. Race and ethnicity were largely absent from GPT outputs unless explicitly queried. Overall, the paper argues that experimental narratives can serve as a useful tool for studying human and AI imaginaries, but it is not a study of educational outcomes or classroom interventions.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative text-analysis study, but it is qualitative/correlational rather than an educational intervention trial. It does not evaluate learner outcomes or use an RCT/QED design relevant to K-12 efficacy evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable impact on student achievement or educational outcomes. It examines generative AI storytelling properties, so there is no evidence of positive or negative instructional impact for K-12 learners.

interventions.use_case: Comparative analysis of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 story generation in response to identical creative-writing prompts, used to examine generative AI behavior rather than tutoring per se.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates AI-generated storytelling quality and originality relative to human crowdsourced writing, not student literacy achievement. GPT-3.5 and especially GPT-4 produced more homogeneous, predictable narratives with less imaginative rhetoric than humans, but GPT-4 was more progressive in gender and sexuality and occasionally introduced innovative twists such as polyamory or blackmail. No learning outcome or effect size was reported; the comparison is based on qualitative narratological analysis of 250 human stories and 80 GPT stories.
finding.measure: Narrative quality, originality, thematic diversity, and gender/sexuality representation in story continuations
finding.study_size: n=330 stories total (250 human, 80 GPT; plus 50 Llama 3 comparisons mentioned)
